glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 11 shows that the LORD weighs honest dealing and the heart alike, that righteousness delivers the upright while the wicked are snared by their own sin, and that a righteous, generous life blesses its neighbors and city and becomes a tree of life to others.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The chapter continues Solomon’s first collection of two-line sayings (10:1–22:16). Chapter 10 lingered over the mouth; chapter 11 opens in the marketplace, at the scales a merchant uses to weigh goods.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, And he who wins souls is wise.” (Proverbs 11:30)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 11 begins where people do business. “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, But a just weight is His delight” (11:1). The same pairing comes back in verse 20, now about the inner life: the perverse heart is an abomination, “But the blameless in their ways are His delight.” The LORD who notices a thumb on the scale also sees the motive behind it, and He is moved by honesty as well as offended by fraud.

Between those sayings, the chapter moves outward. First comes the person himself. Integrity guides the upright, and riches buy nothing “in the day of wrath” (11:4). The wicked man needs no outside enemy, for he “will fall by his own wickedness,” and the unfaithful are “caught by their lust” (11:5–6). Then come the neighbor and the city, which rejoice or suffer according to the people who live there (11:9–14). Last comes the purse, held open or clenched shut (11:24–28).

The chapter gathers all of this into one image: “The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life” (11:30). Wisdom herself was called a tree of life in 3:18, and the tree lost in Eden is finally restored in Christ (Revelation 22:2). A righteous life is never only for itself. It feeds those around it.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 11:1–8 — Integrity and Righteousness Deliver

The chapter starts with honest weights and a humble heart, then follows each way to its end: integrity keeps the upright on course and righteousness rescues them, while the wicked trip over their own wickedness and watch their hopes die with them. Wealth buys nothing in the day of wrath, and the trouble meant for the righteous lands on the wicked instead.

Proverbs 11:9–15 — Neighbors, the City, and Faithful Speech

These sayings trace how one life reaches others: a hypocrite’s words can ruin a neighbor, the upright lift up a city, and the mouth of the wicked can tear it down. Wisdom here is quiet and trustworthy, holding its tongue instead of belittling a neighbor, keeping a confidence, seeking many counselors, and refusing a rash pledge for a stranger’s debt.

Proverbs 11:16–23 — The Sure Reward of Righteousness

Every person ends up holding what he valued, so the sayings set a gracious woman’s honor against the riches of ruthless men, mercy’s blessing against cruelty’s self-inflicted harm, and the sure harvest of sowing righteousness against the deceptive wages of the wicked. The LORD’s delight in the blameless returns from 11:1, and the jarring picture of a gold ring in a pig’s snout warns that beauty without discretion is wasted, a principle that holds for men as well.

Proverbs 11:24–31 — Generosity and the Fruit of the Righteous

Open hands are refreshed and multiplied while the hoarder of grain is cursed and the one who leans on riches falls, a pattern of God’s world that commends generosity without promising a financial return. The righteous flourish like green leaves and bear fruit that gives life to others, and the closing saying argues that if even the righteous are repaid on the earth, the ungodly and the sinner surely will be.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 11 brings the LORD into the places where money changes hands. A rigged scale, a pledge for a stranger’s debt, grain held back while people go hungry, and a fortune someone leans on are all things God weighs (11:1, 15, 26, 28). Because these sayings describe how God’s world generally works, they commend honesty and generosity without turning giving into an investment or poverty into proof of sin.

The chapter also closes with sober weight. If even the righteous are “recompensed on the earth,” including the LORD’s discipline, the ungodly cannot expect to escape (11:31). Peter quotes the verse in its Greek form, “If the righteous one is scarcely saved, Where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (1 Peter 4:18), while urging suffering believers to keep entrusting their souls to a faithful Creator.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Honesty God delights in. The LORD detests dishonest scales and a perverse heart, and He delights in a just weight and a blameless walk (11:1, 3, 20).

Sin as its own snare. The wicked fall by their own wickedness, are caught by their own desires, and pursue evil to their own death, while the cruel trouble their own flesh (11:5–6, 17, 19, 27).

The righteous among their neighbors. Speech, silence, kept confidences, and wise counsel decide whether a neighbor and a city are helped or harmed (11:9–14).

Open hands and closed hands. Scattering, watering, and selling grain bring blessing, while withholding and trusting in riches lead to poverty, a curse, and a fall (11:24–26, 28).

What riches cannot do. Wealth cannot deliver in the day of wrath, and the honor of the gracious and the sure reward of the righteous outlast it (11:4, 16, 18, 28).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Abomination and delight (11:1, 20). What the LORD finds detestable, set beside what gives Him pleasure. Proverbs often pairs the two, and here the pairing reaches from the marketplace to the heart.

Integrity (11:3). Wholeness of life, the same person inside and out. The upright are guided by it when choices are hard, while the crooked ways of the unfaithful destroy them.

The day of wrath (11:4). The time when God’s judgment falls, most likely as it comes in history or at death. Money has no value on that day.

Surety (11:15). One who pledges to pay another person’s debt. The warning repeats the father’s counsel in 6:1–5 against rash pledges; it is not a ban on helping others.

The tree of life (11:30). An image from Eden first used of Wisdom in 3:18. The fruit of a righteous life gives nourishment and life to others, and in Christ the tree of life is restored to His people (Revelation 2:7).

He who wins souls (11:30). The Hebrew is literally “takes lives,” an expression that can elsewhere mean to kill, but here it is positive and is usually understood as winning or gaining people. The words rightly apply to bringing others to God, though the saying is broader than a command about evangelism.

sections.title: Neighbors, the City, and Faithful Speech
Generosity and the Fruit of the Righteous

1.brief: God cares about the marketplace. Dishonest scales used to cheat a buyer are “an abomination to the LORD,” something He finds detestable, while an honest weight is “His delight,” so ordinary trade is carried on under His eye.
1.explain:
“Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD,”

Trade in Israel ran on balance scales and stone weights. A merchant could cheat by using a lighter stone when he sold and a heavier one when he bought, and the customer would never know. The Law had already forbidden it: “You shall have honest scales, honest weights” (Leviticus 19:36). Proverbs calls such scales “an abomination to the LORD,” something He finds detestable. That is strong language for a market trick, and it is meant to be. God does not treat cheating in business as a small matter, because it wrongs a neighbor in secret and lies about the value of things.

“But a just weight is His delight.”

The contrast is just as strong in the other direction. An honest weight is “His delight.” God is not only offended by fraud; He takes pleasure in honesty. The ordinary work of buying and selling is carried on under His eye, and a fair deal at a market stall pleases Him. This is wisdom as skill for living applied to work and money: doing business in a way God enjoys. The same pairing of abomination and delight returns in 11:20, where it is applied to the heart.
1.notes:
The 1611 King James Version gives the Hebrew of two phrases in its margin. For its “false balance” (the NKJV’s “Dishonest scales”) it notes balances of deceit, and for “a just weight” it notes a perfect stone, that is, a whole, full-weight stone. The Hebrew word for a weight is the ordinary word for a stone, because weights were stones carried in a bag (compare Deuteronomy 25:13, “differing weights, a heavy and a light”).

Proverbs returns to the subject in 16:11 and in 20:10 and 20:23, where “Diverse weights” are again called “an abomination to the LORD.”

2.brief: Pride comes in, and shame follows close behind it. Wisdom is found with the humble, who know their limits and stay teachable, so humility is the ground where wisdom grows.
2.explain:
“When pride comes, then comes shame;”

Pride and shame arrive together, one right behind the other. Pride is an inflated view of oneself that refuses to admit limits or take correction. It promises honor, but it brings the opposite. The proud person overreaches, refuses advice, and sooner or later is exposed and brought low. Proverbs will say it again: “Pride goes before destruction” (16:18).

“But with the humble is wisdom.”

The humble are modest about themselves and know their limits. Because they do not think they know everything, they stay teachable, and so wisdom is found with them. Humility is the ground where wisdom grows. The saying fits the fear of the LORD, which begins with a right view of God and therefore a right view of oneself. Proverbs says elsewhere that the LORD “gives grace to the humble” (3:34). Pride receives shame; humility receives wisdom.
2.notes:
In Hebrew the two key words of the first line sound alike: the word for pride is zadon and the word for shame is qalon. The matching sound ties the two words together, so the ear hears shame arriving with pride just as the line says it does, and the saying becomes easy to remember.

The Hebrew word for “humble” occurs only here in the Old Testament and means modest. A verb from the same root appears in Micah 6:8, “to walk humbly with your God,” where it describes a lowly, modest walk before God. The humble of this verse have that same modesty, which keeps them teachable.

3.brief: Integrity works like a guide for the upright, keeping them on course when choices are hard. The crooked dealing of the unfaithful does the opposite, leading them toward their own destruction.
3.explain:
“The integrity of the upright will guide them,”

Integrity is wholeness, being the same person inside and out. For the upright it works like a guide. When choices are hard or confusing, integrity already knows what it will not do, and that keeps them on course. They do not need to calculate every angle, because they are not looking for a way around what is right.

“But the perversity of the unfaithful will destroy them.”

The unfaithful are the treacherous, people who break trust. Their perversity, their crooked and twisted dealing, does the opposite of a guide: it leads them to their own destruction. The same character that drives their choices finally ruins them. The saying shows that a person’s character is not neutral. It either guides or destroys.
3.notes: The Hebrew word for “perversity” means crookedness or crooked dealing, and in the Old Testament it occurs only here and in 15:4. It stands against “upright,” a word whose basic sense is straight. The ESV renders it “crookedness” and the KJV “perverseness.”

4.brief: Wealth cannot buy anything “in the day of wrath,” when God’s judgment comes. Only righteousness delivers from death, echoing the second line of 10:2 and putting money in its true, limited place.
4.explain:
“Riches do not profit in the day of wrath,”

“The day of wrath” is the day when God’s judgment comes, whether in a disaster within history or at death. On that day money cannot buy a way out. The prophet Zephaniah said the same thing about the day of the LORD: “Neither their silver nor their gold Shall be able to deliver them In the day of the LORD’s wrath” (Zephaniah 1:18). Wealth can do many things, but it cannot deal with God.

“But righteousness delivers from death.”

The second line repeats 10:2 word for word. Righteousness, living rightly before God, does what riches cannot. Placed in this chapter, the saying begins a cluster of sayings about deliverance (11:4–9). It also puts money in its true, limited place, a theme the chapter will return to at its end: “He who trusts in his riches will fall” (11:28).
4.notes:
The second line is identical to 10:2b in the NKJV; the first line here replaces “Treasures of wickedness profit nothing” with a reference to the day of wrath.

Deliverance links the sayings of this section: “delivers” (11:4), “deliver” (11:6), “is delivered” (11:8), and “will be delivered” (11:9). The Hebrew uses two different verbs for it, one in 11:4 and 11:6 and another in 11:8 and 11:9, so the link is one of thought carried by related words rather than a single repeated word.

5.brief: A blameless person’s righteousness keeps his road straight and level before him. The wicked man needs no outside enemy to bring him down; he trips over his own wickedness.
5.explain:
“The righteousness of the blameless will direct his way aright,”

The blameless person is whole and sincere before God. His righteousness makes his road straight and level, clearing the way in front of him. The picture is of a path without hidden pits and sudden turns. Living rightly does not remove every hardship, but it keeps a person from the self-made obstacles that crooked living creates.

“But the wicked will fall by his own wickedness.”

The wicked man needs no outside enemy. He trips over his own wickedness. The very schemes and habits he uses to get ahead become the obstacles that bring him down. This verse and the next show sin becoming its own trap.
5.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “direct his way aright” means to make straight or level, and it is the same verb used in 3:6, “He shall direct your paths.” The 1611 King James Version points this out with the marginal note “Heb. rectifie,” meaning to make right or straight. The ESV says that righteousness “keeps” his way straight.

6.brief: Righteousness rescues the upright, while the unfaithful are trapped by their own lust, caught by the very desires they chased. Together with verse 5, the saying shows sin becoming its own snare.
6.explain:
“The righteousness of the upright will deliver them,”

Righteousness rescues those who live by it. This line nearly repeats the thought of 11:5 and 11:4, and it adds the idea of rescue. The upright are protected by the very life they have chosen.

“But the unfaithful will be caught by their lust.”

The unfaithful, the treacherous, are caught like an animal in a trap. What catches them is their own lust, the craving and greed that drove them. They chased their desires, and their desires became the snare. Together with 11:5, this saying shows that sin is self-defeating. God has made His world so that wickedness tends to undo itself.
6.notes: The Hebrew word for “lust” is the same word translated “desire” in 10:3. It means a craving, usually an evil one, though it can also mean ruin. The ESV says the treacherous are “taken captive” by their lust, and the KJV renders the word “naughtiness” in its older sense of wickedness.

7.brief: Death ends everything the wicked man was hoping for. His expectations rested on this life and on his own schemes, so when he dies, his hope perishes with him.
7.explain:
“When a wicked man dies, his expectation will perish,”

Death ends everything the wicked man was counting on. His expectations were tied to this life, to his schemes, his wealth, and his plans. When he dies, they die with him. Nothing he hoped for reaches past the grave.

“And the hope of the unjust perishes.”

The second line repeats the first in different words, which drives the point home. The hope of the unjust perishes. This verse looks back to 10:28, “the expectation of the wicked will perish,” and shows what that means at the end of a life. By contrast, the hope of the righteous rests on God, which is why it can end in gladness.
7.notes: The Hebrew word the NKJV renders “the unjust” is a plural form that can come from a noun meaning strength or wealth, or from a similar-looking word meaning wickedness. The NKJV and KJV take it in the second sense. The ESV takes it as the expectation of “wealth,” and the 1984 NIV as what he expected from his “power.” Either way the second line restates the loss of everything the wicked man relied on.

8.brief: The righteous person is rescued out of trouble, and the trouble falls on the wicked instead. The saying pictures a reversal like Haman hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai (Esther 7:10).
8.explain:
“The righteous is delivered from trouble,”

The righteous person is rescued out of trouble. The saying does not say the righteous never face trouble; they are delivered from it. God brings them through and out.

“And it comes to the wicked instead.”

The trouble does not disappear. It lands on the wicked in place of the righteous. Scripture tells this kind of reversal more than once. In the book of Esther, the gallows Haman built for Mordecai became his own: “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (Esther 7:10). The saying reflects God’s justice, which often turns evil back on those who planned it.
8.notes:
The KJV says the wicked comes in his stead, and the ESV that the wicked “walks into” the trouble, both bringing out the idea of one taking the other’s place.

Proverbs 11:9–15 — Neighbors, the City, and Faithful Speech

9.brief: The hypocrite uses his mouth to ruin his neighbor with flattery, lies, or slander. The righteous are delivered through knowledge, seeing through his words and escaping the harm he intends.
9.explain:
“The hypocrite with his mouth destroys his neighbor,”

The hypocrite is the godless person who hides his real character behind a pleasant face. His weapon is his mouth. With flattery, lies, rumors, or false advice, he can ruin the person who lives next to him and trusts him. The damage is real, though no blow is struck. The section opens here because the next several sayings trace how one person’s life and speech reach the people around him.

“But through knowledge the righteous will be delivered.”

The righteous escape “through knowledge.” They know the truth, know God’s ways, and can see through smooth words, so the hypocrite’s mouth does not take them in. Knowledge here is a protection. The deliverance theme of 11:4–8 continues, and this time the rescue comes by discernment.
9.notes: The ESV and the 1984 NIV render “The hypocrite” as “the godless,” the sense of the Hebrew word, which describes a person estranged from God rather than only a pretender.

10.brief: A whole city feels the fortunes of the righteous and the wicked. When the righteous prosper the city rejoices, and when the wicked perish people shout for joy, because both kinds of lives touch the common good.
10.explain:
“When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices;”

A whole city feels the fortunes of its people. When the righteous prosper, the city is glad, because their success benefits others. They deal honestly, help their neighbors, and use their influence for good. Their well-being spreads to the common good.

“And when the wicked perish, there is jubilation.”

When the wicked fall, people shout for joy. This is not cruelty but relief. The wicked had been a burden on the community through oppression, fraud, and fear, and their removal lifts that weight. Proverbs says the same of rulers: “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice; But when a wicked man rules, the people groan” (29:2). Both kinds of lives touch everyone around them.
10.notes: The word “jubilation” translates a Hebrew word for a ringing shout of joy. The ESV renders it with “shouts.”

11.brief: Verse 10 finds its explanation here. The good that the upright bring to a community lifts a city up, while the mouth of the wicked, with its lies and stirring of strife, can overthrow it.
11.explain:
“By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted,”

This saying explains the one before it. The upright bring blessing to a community, through their honest work, their wise counsel, their prayers, and the good they do. That blessing lifts a city up and makes it a better place to live. Proverbs says it on a larger scale: “Righteousness exalts a nation” (14:34).

“But it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked.”

The wicked can tear a city down, and the instrument named here is the mouth. Lies, slander, false promises, and words that stir up strife can break apart what took years to build. This verse continues the concern of 11:9: what the hypocrite’s mouth does to a neighbor, the wicked mouth can do to a whole city.

12.brief: Belittling a neighbor shows a lack of wisdom. The man of understanding keeps quiet when he could mock or criticize, guarding both the neighbor’s dignity and the peace between them.
12.explain:
“He who is devoid of wisdom despises his neighbor,”

To despise a neighbor is to look down on him and belittle him, often out loud. Proverbs says this reveals a lack of wisdom, in Hebrew literally a lack of heart. The person who mocks his neighbor shows that he does not understand people, himself, or the value God places on others. He also damages a relationship he will need.

“But a man of understanding holds his peace.”

The man of understanding keeps quiet. He may see the neighbor’s faults, and he may be tempted to criticize, but he holds his tongue. That guards both the neighbor’s dignity and the peace between them. In a chapter concerned with the neighbor and the city, this restraint is part of what keeps a community whole.
12.notes: The KJV margin gives the literal Hebrew of “devoid of wisdom” as destitute of heart, the expression met earlier at 9:4 and 10:13.

13.brief: A talebearer goes around revealing what was told in confidence. Someone with a faithful spirit keeps the matter covered, and trustworthiness with a secret is a true mark of faithfulness.
13.explain:
“A talebearer reveals secrets,”

The talebearer is someone who goes around carrying stories from house to house. Whatever is told to him in confidence, he passes on. The Law forbade this: “You shall not go about as a talebearer among your people” (Leviticus 19:16). A talebearer damages trust, reputations, and friendships, and no one is safe confiding in him.

“But he who is of a faithful spirit conceals a matter.”

The person with a faithful spirit is trustworthy deep down. When something is told to him, he keeps it covered. Being reliable with a secret is a true mark of faithfulness. This is not covering up wrongdoing; it is refusing to spread what is private and harmful. Faithfulness in small matters of speech shows a person’s character.
13.notes: The KJV margin gives the literal Hebrew of “A talebearer” as one who walks about, being a talebearer, which pictures the person going from place to place with his stories. Proverbs repeats the first line in 20:19.

14.brief: Without wise guidance a people stumble and fall. Safety lies in many counselors, because no single person sees everything, and this holds for nations as well as for families and personal decisions.
14.explain:
“Where there is no counsel, the people fall;”

Counsel is wise guidance. Without it, a people stumble and fall. The word “people” suggests a nation or community, and the saying fits the city of the surrounding sayings. When leaders act without advice, or when no one is willing to give honest guidance, the whole community suffers for it.

“But in the multitude of counselors there is safety.”

Safety lies in many counselors. No single person sees everything. Several wise advisers can catch what one would miss, test plans, and warn against danger. This is humility in practice, the opposite of the pride that brings shame (11:2). The principle holds for nations, and it holds just as well for families, churches, and personal decisions.
14.notes:
The Hebrew word for “counsel” means direction or guidance, and it is the same word translated “wise counsel” in 1:5. The ESV renders it “guidance.” A people without that guidance has no one to set its course, and so it falls.

Proverbs repeats the thought in 15:22 and 24:6, which ends with the same phrase, “in a multitude of counselors there is safety.”

15.brief: Pledging oneself for a stranger’s debt invites suffering, as the father warned in 6:1–5. Refusing such a pledge keeps a person secure, which is wise counsel about rash commitments rather than a ban on helping others.
15.explain:
“He who is surety for a stranger will suffer,”

A surety is someone who guarantees another person’s debt, promising to pay if the borrower does not. The father warned his son about this in 6:1–5: “If you have shaken hands in pledge for a stranger” (6:1), get out of it quickly. To do it for a stranger, someone whose character and circumstances you do not know, is to put yourself at the mercy of a person you cannot trust. Such a pledge will bring suffering.

“But one who hates being surety is secure.”

The person who refuses to make such pledges stays secure. This is wise counsel about rash commitments, not a ban on helping people. Proverbs elsewhere commends generosity and kindness to the poor (11:24–25). The point is to avoid putting oneself under an obligation that may destroy one’s household. A wise person can give what he is able to give, rather than signing away what he cannot afford to lose.
15.notes:
The KJV says the surety “shall smart” for it. The 1611 edition notes in its margin that the Hebrew is literally shall be sore broken, and that the Hebrew behind “suretiship” is literally those that strike hands, the gesture that sealed a pledge.

Proverbs 11:16–23 — The Sure Reward of Righteousness

16.brief: A gracious woman gains and keeps honor, while ruthless men gain and keep only riches. Both hold on to something, and the comparison leaves no doubt which possession is worth more.
16.explain:
“A gracious woman retains honor,”

A gracious woman is marked by kindness and charm of character. She gains honor and keeps it. Her honor is not seized; it grows out of the way she treats people, and it stays with her. In a section about what each kind of life finally holds, she stands as the first example.

“But ruthless men retain riches.”

Ruthless men are violent and overbearing. They also hold on to something, but what they hold is only riches, often taken from others by force. The verb is the same in both lines: each grasps and keeps what he has pursued. The comparison leaves no doubt about which possession is worth more. Honor won by kindness outlasts wealth seized by violence, and the next verses explain why.
16.notes:
For “ruthless men” the ESV has “violent men” and the KJV “strong men.”

The Greek Septuagint expands this verse with additional lines that are not in the Hebrew; the NKJV follows the Hebrew.

17.brief: Mercy blesses the one who shows it, doing good to his own soul. Cruelty works the other way and brings trouble on the cruel person’s own flesh, so the way we treat others comes back on ourselves.
17.explain:
“The merciful man does good for his own soul,”

The merciful man shows kindness and loyal love to others. The surprise of the saying is that he also benefits himself. Kindness does good to his own soul, his inner life and his whole person. Mercy guards his heart from the bitterness that hardness breeds, and it is pleasing to God. This is the usual way God’s world answers kindness, not a promise of health or companionship. A merciful person may still be ill, lonely, or in distress, and that does not prove a lack of mercy.

“But he who is cruel troubles his own flesh.”

Cruelty works the other way. The cruel man means to hurt others, but he brings trouble on his own body and life. His harshness comes back on him in broken relationships, in enemies, and in the way God’s world answers cruelty. “Soul” and “flesh” together cover the whole person. The way we treat others returns on ourselves.
17.notes: The ESV reads the verse with the simpler “benefits himself” and “hurts himself.”

18.brief: The wicked man’s work is deceptive, and its wages are as unreliable as the way he earned them. The one who sows righteousness has a sure reward, a harvest that will not disappoint him.
18.explain:
“The wicked man does deceptive work,”

The wicked man’s work is deceptive in two ways. He earns by deceit, and his wages deceive him too. What he gains looks solid but does not last or satisfy. His work rests on lies, and its results are as unreliable as the way he got them.

“But he who sows righteousness will have a sure reward.”

The righteous person is pictured as a farmer who sows. What he plants is righteousness, and his harvest is sure. The reward may take time, as a harvest does, but it will come and it will be real. Paul states the same principle: “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7). The contrast is between deceptive wages and a sure reward.
18.notes: The Hebrew words for “deceptive” and “reward” sound alike: sheqer means a lie or deception, and seker means wages or hire. The first line speaks literally of wages of deception and the second of a wage of truth, so the wordplay sets false wages beside true wages. The ESV renders the first line with “deceptive wages.”

19.brief: Righteousness and evil each lead somewhere. Just as righteousness leads to life, the one who chases evil is running toward his own death, even if he cannot see where the road ends.
19.explain:
“As righteousness leads to life,”

Righteousness is a road, and it leads somewhere: to life. Proverbs has said this many times (10:16; 10:17). Life here means the full life God gives, including length of days and His favor, set against the death that awaits the other road.

“So he who pursues evil pursues it to his own death.”

The other person is chasing evil, running hard after it. He thinks he is chasing pleasure or gain, but what he is really pursuing is his own death. He may not see where the road ends, but the end is fixed. The two lines show that everyone is going somewhere, and that the direction of a life matters more than how fast a person is moving.
19.notes: The first Hebrew word of the verse can be read as “so” or “thus,” as in the NKJV and KJV, or as a word meaning right, true, or firm, as in the ESV, which speaks of one who is steadfast in righteousness. Either reading sets life against death.

20.brief: The abomination-and-delight pairing of verse 1 returns, now applied to the heart. The LORD detests a perverse heart, but those who walk blamelessly are His delight, so He cares about the inner person as surely as about honest scales.
20.explain:
“Those who are of a perverse heart are an abomination to the LORD,”

The abomination-and-delight pairing of 11:1 returns, but now it is applied to the heart. A perverse heart is twisted and crooked inside. The LORD detests it. He cares about the inner person as surely as He cares about honest scales. Dishonest weights and crooked hearts belong together, because the cheating hand comes from the twisted heart.

“But the blameless in their ways are His delight.”

Those who walk blamelessly, whole and sincere in their conduct, are His delight. The verse moves from heart to ways, from the inside to the walk. God is not only a judge who detests evil; He takes pleasure in people who walk with integrity. The repetition of “His delight” from 11:1 links honest business and an honest heart as the same kind of life.
20.notes: The same two Hebrew words, “abomination” and “delight,” are set against each other in 11:1, in this verse, and again in 12:22 and 15:8.

21.brief: Even when the wicked join hands to protect one another, they will not escape punishment. The descendants of the righteous, by contrast, will be delivered; as a proverb, this describes how the blessing of a godly life commonly reaches the next generation, not an automatic protection for every child of a righteous parent.
21.explain:
“Though they join forces, the wicked will not go unpunished;”

The wicked may band together, join hands, and protect one another, but they will not escape punishment. No alliance can shield them from God’s justice. The point is certainty: however strong the wicked appear as a group, judgment will reach them.

“But the posterity of the righteous will be delivered.”

The descendants of the righteous will be delivered. The blessing of a godly life commonly reaches the next generation. Children raised by righteous parents receive an example, teaching, prayer, and often protection from the consequences that wickedness brings on a family. Proverbs says elsewhere, “The righteous man walks in his integrity; His children are blessed after him” (20:7). This describes how God’s blessing commonly works, not an automatic protection for every child of a righteous parent. Each person still answers for his own way.
21.notes: The phrase “Though they join forces” is literally hand to hand in Hebrew, as the KJV has it. Other versions take the phrase as an expression of certainty: the ESV reads “Be assured,” and the NASB “Assuredly,” and the 1984 NIV opens the verse with a similar assurance.

22.brief: The picture is jarring on purpose: a gold ring in a pig’s snout. Beauty without discretion is just as out of place and wasted, and the principle holds for men as well as women.
22.explain:
“As a ring of gold in a swine’s snout,”

The picture is jarring on purpose. A gold nose ring was a piece of women’s jewelry; when Abraham’s servant found Rebekah, he says, “I put the nose ring on her nose” (Genesis 24:47). Now imagine that ring in the snout of a pig, an unclean animal rooting in the mud. The gold is real and valuable, but it is completely out of place.

“So is a lovely woman who lacks discretion.”

Beauty without discretion is just as out of place and wasted. Discretion is good judgment and moral sense, knowing what is fitting. Without it, outward loveliness is attached to a life that drags it through the dirt. The saying is not an insult to women, and it does not make women the problem. The principle holds for men just as well; honor is no more fitting for a fool (26:1). The book closes by saying that “beauty is passing,” and that the woman who fears the LORD is the one to be praised (31:30).
22.notes: The Hebrew word for “discretion” means taste, and by extension judgment, a sense of what is fitting. The line says literally that the woman turns aside from taste. The 1611 King James Version, which reads “without discretion,” gives the Hebrew in its margin as “departeth from.” She has the beauty, but she has turned away from the judgment that would make it fitting.

23.brief: The righteous desire only what is good, and their longing ends in good. What the wicked can expect is wrath, because judgment is where their path leads.
23.explain:
“The desire of the righteous is only good,”

The righteous desire what is good, and their longing ends in good. Because their desires are formed by God’s ways, they reach for good things, and in the end they receive good. This continues the thought of 10:24, where “the desire of the righteous will be granted.”

“But the expectation of the wicked is wrath.”

The wicked also look forward, but what they can expect is wrath. Whatever they hope for, judgment is where their path leads. This sharpens 10:28 and 11:7, where the expectation of the wicked perishes. Here it does more than perish; it is replaced by wrath. The section closes as it has run, with each person finally holding what his life pursued.
23.notes:
The ESV says the desire of the righteous “ends only” in good, taking the verse as a statement about outcomes.

Proverbs 11:24–31 — Generosity and the Fruit of the Righteous

24.brief: Generosity works by a paradox: one person scatters freely and yet gains more, while another holds back more than is right and still ends in poverty. Giving does not drain a life the way hoarding does, though the saying describes a pattern rather than a financial formula.
24.explain:
“There is one who scatters, yet increases more;”

The picture is of a farmer scattering seed, or of a person scattering his goods freely to others. By ordinary arithmetic he should end up with less, yet he “increases more.” Generosity works by a paradox in God’s world. What is given away freely does not drain a life the way people expect. The generous person is enriched in relationships, in trust, and under God’s blessing, and often in material ways as well.

“And there is one who withholds more than is right, But it leads to poverty.”

The other person holds back “more than is right,” keeping what he should have given or paid. He expects to protect his wealth, but his stinginess “leads to poverty.” Hoarding does not secure a life; it shrinks it. The saying describes a pattern of God’s world, not a financial formula. It commends an open hand without promising that every gift will be returned in money.
24.notes: This verse has three lines in the NKJV rather than the usual two. The ESV says that the one who withholds “suffers want.”

25.brief: The generous soul will be made rich, and the one who waters others will be watered himself. Refreshment given returns to the giver under God’s care, the principle Paul applies to sowing and reaping in giving (2 Corinthians 9:6), though the saying commends generosity without promising a financial return.
25.explain:
“The generous soul will be made rich,”

In Hebrew the generous person is literally a soul of blessing, someone whose life brings blessing to others. That person “will be made rich,” or in the older image, made fat, a picture of abundance and health in a land where food was never guaranteed. The blessing a generous person gives comes back to him.

“And he who waters will also be watered himself.”

In a dry land, water is life. The one who waters others, refreshing them with help, encouragement, and provision, will be refreshed himself. Paul applies the same principle to giving: “he who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6). The saying commends generosity and describes how God commonly answers it. It does not promise a financial return on every gift, and it should not turn giving into an investment strategy. The point is that generosity does not leave the giver dry.
25.notes: The KJV says that the liberal soul shall be “made fat,” and its margin gives the literal Hebrew of “liberal soul” as soul of blessing.

26.brief: In a time of need, the one who holds back grain from the people earns their curse. The one who sells it to them has blessing on his head, so generosity includes how a person does business when others are in want.
26.explain:
“The people will curse him who withholds grain,”

In a time of shortage, a man with stored grain could hold it back from the market, waiting for prices to climb while people went hungry. The people curse him. His hoarding may be legal, but it is heartless, and the community knows it. Proverbs says elsewhere, “Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor Will also cry himself and not be heard” (21:13).

“But blessing will be on the head of him who sells it.”

The one who sells his grain when people need it has blessing on his head, the same image used in 10:6. He still sells; he is not required to give everything away. But he does business in a way that serves the people in their need. Generosity includes how a person conducts business when others are in want.
26.notes: The NLT expands the second line to make the setting explicit: “but they bless the one who sells in time of need.”

27.brief: Whoever earnestly seeks what is good finds favor along the way. The one who goes looking for evil will find it too, because the trouble he seeks will come back on him.
27.explain:
“He who earnestly seeks good finds favor,”

The verb translated “earnestly seeks” pictures looking hard for something. The person who sets himself to seek what is good, for himself and for others, finds favor along the way. Favor here includes goodwill from people and acceptance from God. He was not chasing favor for its own sake; it comes to him as he pursues good.

“But trouble will come to him who seeks evil.”

The one who goes looking for evil, seeking to harm others, will find it, but not where he expected. The trouble he seeks comes back on him. Each person finds what he is looking for. The saying fits the pattern of the whole chapter, in which a person’s way returns on his own head.
27.notes: The NLT puts the second line vividly: “but if you search for evil, it will find you!”

28.brief: Trust placed in riches will fail, and the one who leans on them will fall. The righteous flourish like green leaves, alive and growing because their life is rooted in something deeper than money.
28.explain:
“He who trusts in his riches will fall,”

To trust in riches is to lean on them for security, identity, and safety. Riches cannot bear that weight. The person who leans on them will fall, because wealth can disappear, cannot buy life in “the day of wrath” (11:4), and cannot replace God. Proverbs does not condemn having money; it warns against trusting it.

“But the righteous will flourish like foliage.”

The righteous are pictured as green leaves on a living tree, fresh and growing. The contrast is between falling and flourishing, perhaps even between a falling leaf and a living one. The righteous flourish because their life is rooted in God. The psalmist describes the righteous man as a tree “Whose leaf also shall not wither” (Psalm 1:3).
28.notes: The ESV compares the righteous to a green “leaf,” while the KJV has “branch.”

29.brief: Whoever brings trouble on his own household will inherit nothing but wind, left with nothing he can hold. Such a fool ends up as servant to the wise of heart.
29.explain:
“He who troubles his own house will inherit the wind,”

A man can bring trouble on his own household through cruelty, greed, or foolish management. Proverbs names greed as one cause: “He who is greedy for gain troubles his own house” (15:27). Such a man “will inherit the wind.” What he leaves himself is nothing, air that cannot be held. The household he should have built up is gone, and he has nothing to show for it.

“And the fool will be servant to the wise of heart.”

The man who troubles his household is a fool, and he ends up serving the wise of heart. Having wasted what he had, he must work for someone who managed well. The two lines describe the slow reversal that folly brings. A household mismanaged ends in servitude, while wisdom builds a house that others depend on.

30.brief: The fruit of a righteous life is a tree of life, giving nourishment and life to others, just as Wisdom herself was called in 3:18; the tree of life is finally restored in Christ (Revelation 22:2). The one who wins souls is wise, gaining people for what is good, and the words rightly apply to bringing others to God.
30.explain:
“The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life,”

The fruit of a righteous life is what it produces: its words, deeds, and influence. That fruit is a tree of life, giving nourishment and life to others. The image goes back to the tree in Eden (Genesis 2:9), and Proverbs has already used it of Wisdom herself: “She is a tree of life to those who take hold of her” (3:18). A righteous life does not feed itself only; it becomes a source of life for those around it.

At the layered level, the tree of life points to Christ. The tree lost in Eden is restored in Him, and the Spirit promises, “To him who overcomes I will give to eat from the tree of life” (Revelation 2:7). The righteous bear life-giving fruit because they are joined to the One who is life.

“And he who wins souls is wise.”

The Hebrew of this line is literally “takes lives” or “takes souls.” Elsewhere the same expression can mean to kill; Proverbs itself says greed “takes away the life of its owners” (1:19). Here it is clearly positive, since the one who does it “is wise.” It is usually understood as winning or gaining people, drawing them to what is good. The wise person, whose life bears fruit like a tree of life, attracts others and wins them to the way of life. The NKJV’s “wins souls” rightly supports applying the words to bringing others to God, an application the rest of Scripture affirms; Daniel 12:3 speaks of “those who turn many to righteousness.” That application is legitimate, but it is secondary; the verse’s first point is that a righteous and wise life draws others toward life.
30.notes:
The KJV margin gives the literal Hebrew of “winneth” as “taketh.” The ESV says the wise man “captures” souls, and the NLT “a wise person wins friends.”

The Greek Septuagint reads the second line very differently, as a statement that the lives of the lawless are taken away before their time. The NKJV follows the Hebrew.

31.brief: The verse argues from the lesser to the greater. If even the righteous are repaid on the earth, including God’s discipline, how much more will the ungodly and the sinner be repaid; Peter draws on the same argument (1 Peter 4:18).
31.explain:
“If the righteous will be recompensed on the earth,”

To be recompensed is to be repaid. “On the earth” means in this life. The verse begins from what the reader already accepts: even the righteous are repaid here, for good and also for wrong. God disciplines those He loves: “For whom the LORD loves He corrects” (3:12). The righteous are not exempt from His dealings with them.

“How much more the ungodly and the sinner.”

The argument moves from the lesser to the greater. If God repays even the righteous, how much more will He repay the ungodly and the sinner. No one should imagine that the wicked will slip through God’s justice. Peter quotes this verse to suffering believers, in the form found in the Greek Septuagint: “If the righteous one is scarcely saved, Where will the ungodly and the sinner appear?” (1 Peter 4:18). The wording differs from the Hebrew, but the argument is the same. Peter draws from it a call to keep trusting God, who judges rightly.
31.notes:
The KJV begins the verse with “Behold,” rendering a Hebrew particle that introduces the first line as a given.

Peter’s quotation follows the Greek translation, which reads “scarcely saved” where the Hebrew has “recompensed on the earth.” The NKJV of each passage translates its own text.
